title: Effect of rapamycin on reversing post-ictal impairments in trace fear learning following a single brief convulsive seizure in rats.
abstract: The postictal period, which immediately follows a seizure, is associated with several incapacitating symptoms or signs, such as psychosis, confusion, paresis, aphasia and memory loss. These symptoms can last from several minutes to even days and can have a negative impact on the quality of life for people living with epilepsy. However, there is a scarcity of data concerning the neurobiological mechanisms that mediate postictal amnesia and behavioural impairments. In the present study, we examined the impact of a single brief, self-limiting convulsive seizure induced by the chemoconvulsant pentylenetetrazol (PTZ) on trace fear learning. We found that PTZ administration produced a rapid but transient increase in hippocampal PI3K-Akt-mTOR signalling, with phosphorylation of Akt, mTOR, and ribosomal protein S6 peaking between 2 and 6 h post-seizure and returning to baseline by 24 h. This activation coincided with increased expression of plasticity-related markers, including Egr1 and PSD-95, and was associated with impaired memory in a hippocampus-dependent trace fear conditioning task. Administration of the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin 30 min post-seizure rescued the memory deficit. These findings suggest that postictal hyperactivation of mTOR signalling disrupts mechanisms of synaptic plasticity through excessive or unregulated protein synthesis, potentially saturating plasticity mechanisms and impairing new memory formation. Taken together, our results identify a critical role for aberrant mTOR signaling in mediating postictal cognitive dysfunction and suggest that targeted inhibition of mTORC1 may represent a therapeutic strategy for preserving memory after seizures.

title: Phubbing and social media addiction in patients with epilepsy: A cross-sectional case-control study.
abstract:
Problematic smartphone use, phubbing behavior, and social media addiction have emerged as important behavioral concerns. Although psychiatric comorbidities are common in epilepsy, data regarding digital behavioral addictions in epilepsy remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate phubbing, smartphone addiction, and social media addiction in adults with epilepsy (AWE) compared with healthy controls and to investigate their associations with psychological and epilepsy-related clinical variables.
This cross-sectional case-control study included 102 AWE and 102 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Participants completed validated scales assessing phubbing, social media addiction, smartphone addiction, depression, and anxiety. Correlation analyses and bootstrap-based path analyses were performed.
Healthy controls demonstrated significantly higher general phubbing, nomophobia, smartphone addiction, and social media addiction scores than AWE (all p < 0.01). In contrast, AWE had significantly higher depressive symptom scores (p < 0.001). Anxiety symptoms emerged as the strongest predictor of behavioral addiction-related measures in both groups. Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale - Anxiety subscale (HADS-A) scores significantly predicted general phubbing, smartphone addiction, and social media addiction in both AWE and healthy controls (all p < 0.001). Epilepsy-related clinical variables showed minimal associations with problematic digital behaviors. TikTok use was significantly more prevalent among AWE than healthy controls (23.5% vs. 3.9%, p < 0.001).
AWE did not demonstrate greater problematic smartphone or social media use compared with healthy controls, despite exhibiting higher depressive symptom burden. Anxiety symptoms appeared to represent the principal correlate of problematic digital engagement independent of epilepsy-related clinical characteristics.

title: Temporal lobe epilepsy and depression: a dysfunctional lobe overshadows a sclerotic hippocampus.
abstract: Depression is one of the most frequent psychiatric comorbidities in drug-resistant patients with epilepsy, reaching up to 60% of them. Studies indicate that the pathophysiology of depression and epilepsy have a lot in common, especially the temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). Since hippocampal sclerosis (HS) is a frequent histopathology finding in patients with TLE, the purpose of this study was to investigate if there is a frequency relation between depression and the different types of HS. 119 patients with TLE, with and without HS, were selected (HS1 = 40, HS2 = 40, NHS = 39) and their medical records were analyzed. Depression was seen in 44 of them, without difference between HS types nor NHS (HS1 = 20, HS2 = 12, NHS = 12, p = 0.1). However, women were 3 times more likely to have depression (p = 0.004). Patients without HS were younger at seizure onset than those with HS2 (p = 0.02). The HS2 group had more cases of initial precipitating injury than NHS (p < 0.001) but were similar to HS1 patients. Our study shows that presence of depression in drug-resistant patients with mesial temporal lobe epilepsy is linked to hippocampal disfunction rather than neuronal density in the hippocampus.

title: Altered EEG microstate dynamics reflect depressive symptoms in temporal lobe epilepsy.
abstract:
Depressive symptoms are a common and disabling comorbidity in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), yet the neural mechanisms linking seizure networks to affective symptoms remain unclear. Although limbic network dysfunction has been implicated in both epilepsy and depressive disorders, it is unknown whether the time-varying dynamics of large-scale electrophysiological brain states reflect depressive symptom severity in TLE. In this study, we examined whether EEG microstate dynamics capture network alterations associated with depressive symptoms in individuals with unilateral TLE.
We analyzed resting-state, visually normal scalp EEG from 26 individuals with unilateral TLE. EEG microstates were identified by clustering global field power peaks into four canonical classes, with electrode positions mirrored to align the ictal hemisphere across subjects. Microstate dwell time, fractional occupancy, global transition entropy, and Markov transition probabilities were quantified and related to Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI) scores.
Individuals with high depressive symptoms (BDI ≥ 13; N = 12) exhibited longer mean dwell time in the ictal hemisphere-aligned microstate compared with individuals with low depressive symptom burden (BDI < 13; N = 14). Across subjects, dwell time in this microstate correlated with depressive symptom severity (r = 0.57, p = 0.002). TLE individuals with higher depressive symptoms exhibited reduced global transition entropy (p = 0.02), which also correlated with depressive symptom severity (r = -0.54, p = 0.004), indicating decreased flexibility of microstate transitions. Despite similar fractional occupancy of this state between groups, individuals with higher depressive symptoms were less likely to transition into the ictal hemisphere-aligned microstate from non-ictal or posterior configurations. Once engaged, however, the ictal-aligned microstate showed increased persistence, indicating prolonged stabilization of this network configuration.
Higher depressive symptom burden in unilateral TLE is associated with increased temporal rigidity of the ictal hemisphere-aligned brain microstate, reflecting impaired disengagement of epileptogenic network configurations. These findings suggest that depressive symptoms in TLE may be associated with epilepsy-related disruptions in large-scale neural dynamics.

title: Comparative efficacy of first-line antiseizure monotherapy in pediatric focal epilepsy: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
abstract:
First-line antiseizure medication (ASM) monotherapy remains the recommended initial treatment for pediatric focal epilepsy. Although several ASMs are available, uncertainty persists regarding their comparative efficacy, safety, and tolerability, particularly in children. This umbrella review aimed to synthesize and map the available evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses evaluating first-line ASM monotherapies for focal epilepsy, with a focus on informing pediatric treatment decisions.
This umbrella review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses evaluating first-line ASM monotherapy for focal epilepsy were identified through comprehensive database searches. Data on study characteristics, patient populations, ASM comparisons, epilepsy subtypes, follow-up duration, efficacy, safety, and tolerability outcomes were extracted and synthesized descriptively. Evidence mapping was performed to summarize the findings, and potential overlap of primary studies across the included reviews was considered. Where available, outcome-specific certainty-of-evidence ratings reported by the source reviews using GRADE or CINeMA were also extracted and summarized.
Sixteen systematic reviews and meta-analyses were included, comprising randomized controlled trials and individual participant data analyses from pediatric and mixed-age populations. Frequently evaluated ASMs included carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, valproate, phenytoin, and several newer-generation agents. Across the included reviews, no single first-line ASM showed consistent superiority for seizure control outcomes. Selected comparisons suggested tolerability advantages for lamotrigine, levetiracetam, and some newer-generation ASMs; however, these findings were not uniform across outcomes or reviews. Several comparative estimates were imprecise, with confidence intervals encompassing potentially clinically meaningful effects, and substantial heterogeneity was present across epilepsy subtype definitions, patient populations, follow-up durations, and outcome reporting. The frequent inclusion of mixed-age populations further limited the strength and direct applicability of pediatric-specific conclusions.
Current umbrella-level evidence does not establish clear superiority of one first-line ASM over another for seizure control in pediatric focal epilepsy. Importantly, the absence of statistically significant differences should not be interpreted as evidence of therapeutic equivalence, because several estimates remain imprecise and clinically meaningful differences cannot be excluded. Interpretation is further limited by the scarcity of pediatric-specific comparative data, the frequent inclusion of mixed-age populations, and methodological and outcome heterogeneity across reviews. Safety and tolerability should therefore be considered alongside efficacy when individualizing treatment selection. Well-designed pediatric-specific comparative studies using standardized outcome measures are needed to strengthen evidence-based treatment recommendations.

title: Effect of cognitive enhancement therapy for early course schizophrenia on gray matter volume: A confirmatory multisite randomized clinical trial.
abstract:
Cognitive Enhancement Therapy (CET) is an evidence-based cognitive remediation intervention for early course schizophrenia with established benefits for cognition. CET may protect against broad temporolimbic gray matter volume loss associated with cognitive improvement, but this finding has yet to be replicated. This research reexamined if CET protects against temporolimbic gray matter volume loss in an independent and larger multisite early course sample, and if this neuroprotective effect predicts cognitive and social adjustment improvement.
Ninety-nine participants with early course schizophrenia completed MRI, cognitive, and social adjustment assessments at baseline, 9 (mid-treatment), and 18 (end of treatment) months. Linear mixed-effects models examined the differential impact of CET (n = 56) compared to Enriched Supportive Therapy (n = 43) on temporolimbic gray matter volume in regions-of-interest (ROIs) that previously demonstrated CET-related neuroprotection (primary ROIs), as well as frontotemporal ROIs outlined in the first trial (secondary ROIs).
The right rostral anterior cingulate was the only primary ROI to demonstrate a significant group × time interaction, but was unrelated to cognitive and social adjustment change. No secondary ROIs exhibited a differential treatment effect.
This confirmatory trial did not recapitulate the observed broad pattern of CET-related temporolimbic gray matter volume neuroprotection. Consistent with the larger literature demonstrating limited evidence of cognitive remediation effects on the brain in schizophrenia, these findings underscore the need for continued investigation of CET-related changes with other neuroimaging modalities, especially given its established cognitive benefits. Such information is critical for cognitive remediation optimization based on validated therapeutic mechanisms.

title: Brain and Cardiometabolic Effects of Major Weight Loss in People With Obesity: Preliminary Cohort Findings.
abstract:
Given the overlap between obesity-related metabolic and vascular abnormalities and Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk factors, it is critical to determine whether weight loss improves brain and cardiovascular health. This study examined whether ≥ 40% excess-weight loss is associated with improvements in cardiometabolic risk, brain structure, and cognition.
The study was a longitudinal study of individuals with obesity undergoing metabolic and bariatric surgery or medical/behavioral weight-loss treatment. Participants were classified at follow-up as weight-loss (WL; ≥ 40% excess-weight loss) or non-weight-loss (nWL; < 40%). All completed medical evaluations, structural MRI, and cognitive testing at baseline and 1 year.
At 1 year, the WL group exhibited improvements in BMI, HbA1C, inflammatory, metabolic, and lipid profiles. MRI-based volumetrics revealed increases in subcortical gray-matter volume and preservation of AD-vulnerable regions. Cognitive performance remained unchanged.
Achieving ≥ 40% excess-weight loss was associated with improvements in metabolic health and brain structure, including favorable subcortical volume increases. These findings underscore the potential of sustained weight reduction to mitigate risks linked to metabolic syndromes and neurodegeneration. Longer-term follow-up is warranted to determine whether continued metabolic improvements lead to detectable cognitive gains and additional brain-health benefits beyond 1 year.

title: Taiwanese expert consensus on the assessment and management of agitation in dementia: A modified Delphi study.
abstract:
Agitation in dementia is clinically heterogeneous and requires individualized assessment, nonpharmacological strategies, and cautious pharmacological treatment. However, evidence-based consensus guidance addressing the broader care process across different care settings remains limited.
This two-round modified Delphi study was jointly conducted by the Taiwanese Society for Geriatric Psychiatry and the Taiwan Dementia Society. A working group developed preliminary statements based on targeted evidence review, statement-level evidence assessment, and clinical relevance to Taiwan. A panel of 30 experts, including 20 geriatric psychiatrists and 10 neurologists, participated in structured discussion, anonymous prioritization voting, post-round revision, and final anonymous voting. Consensus thresholds were predefined for evidence-based recommendations and good practice statements (GPS).
Of 14 preliminary statements generated by the working group, 10 were retained and organized into three clinical domains: diagnosis and assessment, nonpharmacological management, and pharmacological management by the panel. Four statements were classified as GPS, and six were evidence-based recommendations. Two statements received strong recommendations and four received conditional recommendations. All final statements met predefined consensus thresholds, with agreement ranging from 71% to 100%; eight statements achieved agreement of 90% or higher. The consensus supports structured assessment, identification of contributing factors, nonpharmacological and community-based care when feasible, pharmacological treatment only in clinically appropriate situations, and low-dose, short-term medication use with regular reassessment.
The consensus provides a practice-oriented framework for the assessment and management of agitation in dementia within the Taiwanese healthcare context. It may support stepwise clinical decision-making while identifying areas requiring further agitation-specific evidence.

title: A systematic review of Mendelian randomization evidence on alcohol-related phenotypes and multiple human diseases.
abstract:
This systematic review synthesises Mendelian randomization (MR) studies to evaluate genetic evidence for the role of alcohol consumption across multiple health domains.
We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO for MR studies on alcohol phenotypes and health outcomes. Eligible studies used genetic variants as instruments for alcohol phenotypes such as alcohol consumption, alcohol use disorder, or Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test scores. MR investigations were classified as single-variant or multiple-variant studies. We assessed the robustness of evidence as robust, probable, suggestive, insufficient, or non-evaluable. Due to mainly outcome sample overlap we conducted a qualitative synthesis of the evidence.
We identified 88 MR studies covering 630 alcohol-disease investigations and up to 2433,011 participants. Most studies (84.4%) focused on European ancestry populations. Across 14 disease categories, 109 unique outcomes were assessed. We identified 30 robust, 98 probable, and 15 suggestive associations. Robust evidence linked alcohol consumption to increased risks of cardiovascular diseases (e.g., coronary artery disease, stroke, hypertension), several cancers (e.g., breast, colorectal, oropharyngeal, hepatocellular), alcohol-associated liver disease, chronic pancreatitis, Crohn's disease, Parkinson's disease, major depression, and all-cause mortality. An additional 113 probable and suggestive associations extended to other cancers, gastrointestinal, neurological, endocrine, eye, oral, and skin conditions. However, 487 (77%) investigations yielded insufficient or non-evaluable evidence.
The reviewed MR evidence suggests associations between genetic liability to alcohol-related phenotypes and a range of disease and mortality outcomes. However, findings should be interpreted cautiously and supported by complementary causal inference approaches to strengthen causal interpretation.

title: Efficacy and Safety Outcomes of Different Plasma Clozapine and Norclozapine Levels in Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder: A Dose-Response Meta-Analysis Exploring "critical" Levels.
abstract:
A dose-response meta-analysis (DRMA) exploring serum/plasma clozapine and norclozapine concentrations in relation to efficacy and safety outcomes in schizophrenia spectrum disorders is warranted.
PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched through February 16th, 2026. Cohort studies and clinical trials of clozapine-exposed participants were eligible. Linear models were first fitted, followed by exploratory quadratic models estimating population-level concentration-response turning points.
Thirty-four studies including 134,111 participants were included. Quadratic models yielded the following exploratory clozapine turning points: Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale change (535 ng/mL), Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale total change (898 ng/mL), tolerability (707 ng/mL), blood dyscrasia (357 ng/mL), electroencephalogram abnormalities/seizures (452 ng/mL), salivary hypersecretion (225 ng/mL), and tachycardia (503 ng/mL). Certainty was moderate for 11/21 and low for 10/21 outcomes.
These values should not be interpreted as universal therapeutic or toxic thresholds, nor as targets for dose escalation. Rather, they are exploratory vertices derived from heterogeneous studies. Overall, findings support individualized therapeutic drug monitoring and caution against pursuing unduly high clozapine concentrations when additional benefit is uncertain and adverse-event risk may increase.

title: Depression in neurodegenerative disease: neurobiological mechanisms and emerging treatments.
abstract: Depression is one of the most common and disabling neuropsychiatric complications of neurodegenerative diseases. In Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), depressive syndromes affect more than one-third of patients and are associated with accelerated cognitive decline, reduced quality of life, and increased healthcare utilisation. Despite this burden, current antidepressant treatments show little or no efficacy in these populations, suggesting that depression arising in the context of neurodegeneration may reflect distinct underlying neurobiological mechanisms. Emerging evidence from molecular imaging, neuropathology, and cognitive neuroscience indicates disease-specific disruption of monoaminergic, glutamatergic, inflammatory, and reward-related circuits in AD and PD. These alterations may undermine the mechanisms of action of standard antidepressants and contribute to treatment resistance. Yet patients with cognitive impairment are routinely excluded from antidepressant trials, and few high-quality studies have evaluated novel therapies in neurodegenerative disease. In this narrative review, we synthesise current evidence on the neurobiological mechanisms underpinning depression in AD and PD and critically evaluate emerging pharmacological and neuromodulatory therapies targeting glutamatergic, serotonergic, dopaminergic, immune, and circuit-level dysfunction. Here, we highlight that depression in neurodegenerative disease offers a unique and underutilised model for mechanistically guided antidepressant development. We identify how interventions including glutamate modulators, dopaminergic agents, kappa opioid antagonists, immune-modulating therapies, and next-generation brain stimulation approaches may offer therapeutic promise. By aligning treatment development with disease-specific circuit and molecular pathology, this framework may improve outcomes for this neglected population while advancing precision psychiatry more broadly.

title: Comprehensive Multimodal Diagnostics and Rehabilitation in Persistent Post-Concussion Syndrome Following Motor Vehicle Collision.
abstract: Motor vehicle collisions (MVCs) are among the most common mechanisms of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), and a meaningful proportion of affected individuals develop persistent post-concussion syndrome (PPCS) characterized by prolonged multidomain dysfunction. Conventional neuroimaging frequently fails to capture the underlying pathophysiology, leaving clinicians without objective diagnostic evidence. We describe a 57-year-old woman who sustained mTBI in a rear-end MVC in March 2023. Head computed tomography (CT) performed at the emergency department and a subsequent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) were both unremarkable. Despite normal structural neuroimaging, comprehensive multimodal functional assessment identified functional abnormalities across eight domains: vestibular function (videonystagmography (VNG)), cortical electrophysiology (quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG)), pupillary autonomics (automated infrared pupillometry), postural stability (computerized dynamic posturography (CDP)), oculomotor control (saccadometry), cardiac autonomic regulation (24-h heart rate variability (HRV)), olfaction (University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT)), and computerized concussion assessment (C3 Logix). Standardized psychological assessments confirmed moderate depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) = 14), moderate anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) = 12), clinically significant post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms (PTSD Checklist for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) (PCL-5 = 38)), and substantial headache impact (Headache Impact Test-6 (HIT-6) = 58). The patient underwent a 10-modality individualized rehabilitation program. Concussion Symptom Checklist (CSC) scores declined from 92 at initial presentation to 0 by July 2023 (17 weeks post-injury), with near-complete re-resolution to 8 by February 2024 following a transient stress-related exacerbation. When conventional neuroimaging is unremarkable, comprehensive multimodal functional testing may provide evidence consistent with mTBI pathophysiology and help guide targeted rehabilitation. This case illustrates the potential value of a systematic, multimodal approach in PPCS management, while acknowledging that definitive attribution of findings to the index injury is constrained by the single-case design and absence of a pre-injury functional baseline.

title: Histone Modifications at the Intersection of Aging, Neuroinflammation and Metabolism in Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: Aging, neuroinflammation and metabolic dysfunction are tightly intertwined in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but how transient pathological signals become persistent cellular states remains poorly understood. Histone post-translational modifications (PTMs) provide a dynamic interface between extracellular stimuli, cellular metabolism and chromatin state. This Review examines how canonical histone modifications and emerging metabolite-derived acylations regulate inflammatory and stress-responsive programmes across microglia, astrocytes and neurons during aging and AD. We discuss how amyloid-β, tau pathology, metabolic dysfunction and innate immune signaling converge on histone-modifying machinery, and how reciprocal interactions between metabolism and chromatin may stabilize disease-associated cell states. Particular attention is given to cellular senescence and neuroimmune memory, while emphasizing the context dependence of individual histone marks across cell types, genomic regions and disease stages. We further evaluate evidence for causality using three criteria: perturbation, persistence and reversibility. This framework distinguishes chromatin states that accompany ongoing pathology from those capable of sustaining pathological cell states beyond their initiating signals. Finally, we consider therapeutic strategies targeting histone-modifying enzymes, chromatin readers and metabolic inputs to restore chromatin plasticity and promote resolution of chronic neuroinflammation.

title: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells: Context-Dependent resilience and vulnerability.
abstract: Retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) exhibit marked heterogeneity in their susceptibility to injury and disease. Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), a small subset of melanopsin-expressing RGCs involved in non-image-forming visual functions, have emerged as a particularly informative example. In multiple experimental models, ipRGCs show relative resistance to acute insults such as optic nerve injury, excitotoxicity, and mitochondrial dysfuinction. In contrast, functional alterations and degeneration have been reported in aging and in neurodegenerative conditions including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. This apparent discrepancy suggests that ipRGC survival may depend on the nature and duration of the underlying stress. In this review, we summarize current evidence on ipRGC resilience and vulnerability across a range of experimental and pathological contexts. We discuss candidate mechanisms that may contribute to these responses, including sustained activity, calcium handling, metabolic specialization, neurochemical interactions, and gene expression programs. We also consider the role of subtype-specific diversity within the ipRGC population in shaping these outcomes. Finally, we examine the potential of ipRGCs as biomarkers of disease and as a source of insight for neuroprotective strategies. Together, these observations support the view that ipRGC behaviour reflects an interaction between intrinsic cellular properties and the context in which they are engaged.

title: Volumetric and Intrastructural Characterization of the Substantia Nigra Using Optimized Synthetic MR Images Derived From Quantitative T1 Maps at 3 T.
abstract: Accurate imaging of the substantia nigra (SN) is critical for diagnosing and monitoring neurodegenerative conditions like Parkinson's disease. However, conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) struggles to precisely visualize this small structure within the deep brain due to poor intrinsic tissue contrast. Although quantitative MRI (qMRI) captures objective tissue properties with diagnostic value to assess neurodegenerative conditions of the SN, additionally acquiring multiple MRI contrasts inherently requires impractically long scan times. To overcome this, qMRI-derived synthetic MRI uses mathematical signal models to retrospectively generate various synthetic contrast weightings from a single map of quantitative T1-relaxation times (qT1). This study investigated which mathematical transformations of qT1 maps, including an approximation for pseudo-proton spin density (pPSD), are best suited to derive optimized synthetic MRI contrasts for accurate SN analysis. By evaluating six dedicated qT1-derived contrast weightings in healthy subjects, this work demonstrates that a nonlinear, signal-increased pPSD-based synthetic MRI contrast (si4_PSD) yields a favorable balance by significantly enhancing optical contrast while maintaining a sufficient signal-to-noise ratio and preserving contrast-to-noise ratio. The si4_PSD images enabled highly consistent, automated atlas-based segmentation of the SN that significantly outperformed traditional manual delineation, overcoming rater variability and bias from age-dependent contrast changes. Automated segmentation revealed significant sex- and hemisphere-dependent differences in SN volume, whereas qT1 data simultaneously uncovered distinct subregional and asymmetric intrastructural aging patterns. These findings highlight that macrostructural volume and intrastructural tissue properties must be assessed as independent variables. In conclusion, this qT1-based, automated framework offers a highly consistent, scalable approach to SN mapping without extending patient scan times. By clearly separating physiological intrastructural changes affecting MRI contrasts from mistakenly perceived general atrophy, this methodology provides a powerful foundation for developing more precise and objective imaging biomarkers for SN-related neurodegenerative diseases in both research and clinical settings.

title: Inferior Frontal Gyrus Alterations in Freezing of Gait in Parkinson's Disease Without Evidence for Overall Hemispheric Lateralization: A Systematic Review and Activation Likelihood Estimation Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Freezing of gait (FOG) is one of the most debilitating motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD). Prior studies have suggested a potential right-hemispheric preference in the pathophysiology of FOG. Yet, there is limited evidence regarding which brain regions are most consistently associated with FOG and whether these alterations indeed show right-hemispheric lateralization. We aimed to identify brain regions associated with FOG based on multimodal neuroimaging findings and to examine their hemispheric lateralization. A systematic review across multiple neuroimaging modalities was performed, followed by an activation likelihood estimation (ALE) coordinate-based meta-analysis to assess convergent brain alterations in PD patients with FOG (freezers) versus those without FOG (nonfreezers). Hemispheric lateralization was assessed using the distribution of reported stereotactic coordinates. The systematic review included 108 articles, of which 33 were included in the primary ALE meta-analysis. We identified a significant convergent cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) pars opercularis/dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in PD freezers compared with nonfreezers. No evidence of overall hemispheric lateralization was observed based on the distribution of reported coordinates. Our findings identify the right IFG as a consistent neural correlate of FOG, potentially reflecting heightened frontal recruitment, with no clear evidence of hemispheric lateralization. The lack of further consistency in brain regions could reflect the known heterogeneity in the pathophysiology of FOG.

title: Cardiac arrest in an adolescent following an overdose of antidepressants comprising sertraline, quetiapine fumarate, and lamotrigine: Case report.
abstract: Antidepressant overdose is a prevalent method of self-harm in patients with depression including bipolar disorder. According to the published literature, typical adverse effects are seizures, prolonged QT intervals, and arrhythmias, with cardiotoxicity primarily observed in adults. This paper reports the first documented case of an 11-year-old adolescent with depression who ingested a massive overdose comprising sertraline (60 tablets at 50 mg, giving a total dose of 3 g), quetiapine fumarate (50 tablets at 100 mg giving a total dose of 5 g) and lamotrigine (120 tablets at 25 mg giving a total dose of 3 g). At ~ 4 hours post ingestion, the patient developed hypoxemia, hypotension, persistent seizures, resulting in cardiac arrest. This case report offers critical insights into the clinical management of such cases involving pediatric populations.

title: Establishing Potosi Virus as a Human Pathogen: Fatal Neuroinvasive Disease in a B-Cell-Depleted Patient.
abstract:
To establish Potosi virus, a mosquito-borne member of the family Peribunyaviridae, as a neuroinvasive human pathogen.
Case report.
A 37-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis on long-term rituximab developed rapidly progressive dementia. Serial MRI demonstrated progressive generalized atrophy. CSF showed transient, minimal lymphocytic pleocytosis. Extensive infectious, autoimmune, and prion evaluations were unrevealing, but CSF metagenomic sequencing detected all 3 genome segments for Potosi virus. Postmortem examination revealed diffuse meningoencephalitis with T-cell-predominant leptomeningeal and perivascular inflammation. Molecular analyses confirmed multiple nucleotide sequences with >99+% concordance with a known Potosi strain, with widespread viral infection confirmed by immunohistochemistry demonstrating intracellular and extracellular viral antigen. Electron microscopy demonstrated particles of a size consistent with the Peribunyaviridae family. Metagenomic sequencing of RNA extracted from frozen brain tissue identified all 3 Potosi virus gene segments without other infectious entities. Findings were concordant across multiple laboratories and institutions.
Potosi virus can cause fatal neuroinvasive disease in humans, as evidenced by convergent postmortem neuropathologic, molecular, and ultrastructural evidence. Chronic B-cell depletion may increase susceptibility to severe disease with arboviral infections, which may present without conventional CNS inflammatory markers. CSF metagenomic sequencing should be considered in immunocompromised patients with unexplained progressive neurologic decline.

title: Vascular endothelial growth factor A induces proliferation of adult neural progenitor cells in non-neurogenic periventricular regions of the adult mouse hindbrain.
abstract:
In addition to the well-established neurogenic niche of the ventricular-subventricular zone (V-SVZ) of the lateral ventricles, neural stem/progenitor cells (NPCs) have been identified in the periventricular regions (PVRs) throughout the adult mouse ventricular system. The potential role of these NPCs in neuroplasticity or neurorestoration, however, remains largely unexplored.
Given that vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) has been shown to promote stem cell proliferation in the V-SVZ, this study aimed to investigate VEGF-A effects on NPC proliferation in mid- and hindbrain PVRs.
Healthy adult male C57BL/6 mice received continuous intracerebroventricular infusions of VEGF-A or artificial cerebrospinal fluid for 7 days. To label proliferating cells, daily injections of thymidine analogues were administered. Proliferation was assessed in the PVRs of the medial wall of the lateral ventricles, the third ventricle, and the aqueduct/fourth ventricle (hindbrain).
Continuous VEGF-A infusion significantly increased overall cell proliferation in the third ventricle and hindbrain PVRs compared with controls, but not in the medial wall of the lateral ventricles. In hindbrain PVRs, the increase in proliferation was restricted to GFAP + Sox2 + NPCs. In contrast, in the wall of the third ventricle, VEGF-A infusion led to a significant reduction in ependymocyte proliferation, with no specific increase observed in other cell types.
While continuous intracerebroventricular VEGF-A infusion enhances NPC proliferation in mid- and hindbrain PVRs, total counts of proliferating cells remain low, and significant lineage progression is not observed. These findings challenge the proposed neurorestorative role of resident NPCs in these brain regions, particularly in the context of neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's disease.

title: Alzheimer's genetic risk factor CASS4 controls microglial focal adhesion biology and amyloidosis.
abstract: Recent genome-wide association studies have identified numerous Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk genes enriched in microglia, including Crk-associated substrate (Cas) scaffold protein family member 4 (CASS4), which encodes the adaptor protein CASS4. Despite its strong genetic association with AD, the role of CASS4 in disease remains poorly understood. Here, we show that full-body Cass4 deletion in 5xFAD mice increases amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, neuronal dystrophy, and cognitive deficits. Since microglia are the predominant brain-resident cells expressing Cass4, we investigated its role in microglial responses to Aβ pathology. Loss of CASS4 impaired microglial mobilization to Aβ plaques and reduced plaque compaction. Phosphoproteomic analysis of purified microglia revealed marked disruption of focal adhesion signaling following Cass4 deletion. Consistent with this, CASS4 deficiency abrogated in vivo microglial recruitment to injury and in vitro wound healing responses, two processes that are centrally orchestrated by focal adhesion biology. Together, these findings identify CASS4 as a critical regulator of microglial function and focal adhesion biology and suggest that CASS4 may represent a therapeutic target for AD.

title: A general practice-centred model for early diagnosis and management of Alzheimer's disease in Denmark: rationale, evidence and a pragmatic diagnostic approach.
abstract:
Alzheimer's disease is a leading cause of disability among older adults and poses increasing challenges for healthcare systems. In Denmark, demographic changes and healthcare reform are driving greater involvement of primary care in diagnosis and management.
This paper examines the rationale for a general practice-centred model and summarises recent diagnostic developments, including blood-based biomarkers.
Although current disease-modifying therapies show only modest benefit, ongoing research and scalable biomarkers enable earlier and more accessible diagnosis. We propose a pragmatic three-step diagnostic approach for primary care, with structured clinical and cognitive assessment, exclusion of secondary causes including structural neuroimaging, and in the near future, the availability of feasible biomarkers to support diagnosis and guide referral. We also outline key organisational, educational and ethical requirements for implementation.
A general practice-centred model may improve diagnostic timeliness, accessibility and continuity of care if integrated within a robust clinical and ethical framework.

title: Different object features shape mnemonic discrimination in younger and older adults.
abstract: The ability to discriminate experiences in memory is an important indicator of cognitive health in older age and a sensitive marker of hippocampal integrity. Measures of mnemonic discrimination, such as the mnemonic similarity task, have the potential to become early diagnostic tools of Alzheimer's dementia. It is thus important to understand how hippocampus-dependent memory functions interact with nonmnemonic processes to determine mnemonic discrimination performance. In this study, we investigate which features contribute to mnemonic discrimination in younger and older age. First, we found in a sample of younger (n = 93, 20-30 years) and older adults (n = 103, 65-82 years) that age impacted performance on the mnemonic similarity task above and beyond the effect of perceptual discrimination of novel 2D configurative objects. Next, in two experiments, we acquired similarity and feature difference ratings for the mnemonic similarity task lures from younger (n = 25 and n = 47, 19-37 years) and older (n = 25 and n = 47, 65-79 years) adults. Using random forest regression and representational similarity analysis, we found that the two groups exhibited unique similarity rating patterns. Finally, enriching our memory data with the feature information, we showed, on the trial level, that mnemonic decisions of older and younger adults are affected by distinct object features. Altogether, these results provide evidence that older adults perceive the differences in lure images distinctively and they may rely on different levels of representations for mnemonic discrimination. title: Copper-Mediated Radiofluorination of the Excitatory Amino Acid Transporter 2 (EAAT2)-Targeted PET Tracer [18F]RP-115: Alternate Synthetic Method.
abstract: Excitatory amino acid transporter 2 (EAAT2) is a key regulator of extracellular glutamate in the central nervous system. Dysregulated EAAT2 is implicated in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), highlighting EAAT2 as a potential target for PET imaging. We previously reported a multistep radiosynthesis of [18F]RP-115, a CNS-permeable prodrug that undergoes esterase-mediated hydrolysis in the CNS to yield the active EAAT2-binding carboxylate. Motivated by recent advances in copper-mediated radiofluorination (CMRF), we sought to develop a more efficient late-stage radiosynthesis of [18F]RP-115. A two-step radiosynthesis of [18F]RP-115 using CMRF provided [18F]RP-115 in high radiochemical yield (52.8% ± 2.1 %, decay-corrected from starting [18F]fluoride ion, n = 4), high molar activity (355 ± 61 GBq/μmol), and high radiochemical purity (> 99%) with a total synthesis time of 70 min. Chiral HPLC analysis demonstrated that the configuration of the aspartic acid residue remained intact without racemization during both the CMRF and trifluoroacetic acid mediated deprotection. We developed an efficient radiosynthesis of [18F]RP-115 via CMRF, achieving high radiochemical yield and molar activity. This efficient synthesis may serve as a basis for the future implementation of a CMRF-based automated radiosynthesis of [18F]RP-115.

title: Resting-State and Task-State Dual-Paradigm fNIRS Study Reveals Dynamic Alterations in Brain Network Activity in Alzheimer's Disease With Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms.
abstract:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) frequently presents with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), severely impacting prognosis. The dynamic brain network mechanisms remain unclear, and traditional neuroimaging faces limitations. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) offers a unique approach to explore these mechanisms under natural conditions.
To systematically compare brain region activation, signal complexity and network topology in AD patients with and without BPSD using resting-state and verbal fluency task (VFT) fNIRS paradigms.
This cross-sectional study enrolled 48 AD patients (24 with BPSD, 24 without) and 25 normal controls (NC). fNIRS recorded hemodynamic changes in the frontal, temporal, parietal and occipital lobes during rest and VFT. Analyses included activation, time-frequency characteristics, functional connectivity and network topology. Partial correlations assessed links between fNIRS metrics and neuropsychological scores.
In resting state, AD-BPSD showed altered coefficient of variation in left premotor and somatosensory cortices, and elevated information entropy in left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (lDLPFC), versus NC and AD-non-BPSD. Functional connectivity abnormalities emerged between right frontal eye field-left somatosensory cortex, and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC)-left superior temporal gyrus (lSTG) (p < 0.05). During VFT, AD-BPSD had significantly lower lDLPFC and left somatosensory activation versus NC (p < 0.05), but increased signal fluctuation and power in right primary motor cortex (rM1) (p < 0.05), alongside reduced whole-brain clustering coefficient (p = 0.023).
AD-BPSD was associated with altered brain functional patterns across resting and task states, involving sensorimotor and executive networks as well as altered interhemispheric coordination. These fNIRS-derived alterations provide exploratory evidence of altered brain functional patterns associated with BPSD and warrant further investigation in larger longitudinal studies.

title: A Phase 1 Study of MK-1942, a Negative Allosteric Modulator of mGluR2, in Healthy Japanese to Flexibly Assess Factors Including CYP2C19 Phenotype.
abstract: MK-1942 is a negative allosteric modulator of the metabotropic glutamate receptor 2 that was investigated for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease and depression. Nonclinical studies with recombinant human CYPs and genotyped human hepatocytes suggested that CYP2C19 is involved in the metabolism of MK-1942. Given the high incidence of different CYP2C19 polymorphisms in the Japanese population, a Phase 1 single and multiple dose study in healthy Japanese participants provided an opportunity to determine the involvement of CYP2C19 phenotype on the clinical PK of MK-1942. Also, since a first-in-human study in non-Japanese showed a decrease in exposures after administration with high-fat meal, we further tested an effect of low-fat meal on PK in the Japan study. The study was designed with flexibility which enabled dose selection for the multiple dose panels, based on the totality of safety and PK data. Oral administration of single and multiple doses of MK-1942 in Japanese participants was generally well tolerated. AUC0-inf was comparable between fasted and fed (low-fat meal) state. Following a single dose of MK-1942, AUC0-inf was ~70% increased in CYP2C19 poor metabolizer (PM) vs. extensive metabolizer (EM). Therefore, a decision was made to test the multiple dose separately for each CYP2C19 phenotype, rather than grouping them into a single panel. As opposed to the expectation from the single dose result, steady state exposures were similar among CYP2C19 phenotypes. These data supported the subsequent global Phase 2 study to permit a low-fat meal around dosing and no dose adjustment for any CYP2C19 phenotype.

title: Effect of Individualized Music Listening on Anxiety and Behaviors of People With Dementia: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
abstract:
To evaluate the effects of individualized music listening (IML) on anxiety levels and behaviors among older adults with dementia in Taiwan.
The current study was a quasi-experimental study. Thirty-two older adults were recruited through convenience sampling and assigned to either an experimental group (EG; n = 16) or control group (CG; n = 16) based on self-rated importance of music in their lives and personal preferences. Participants were selected from five Dementia Community Services Sites (DCSS). The EG received eight sessions of IML (20 minutes per session, twice per week for 4 weeks), whereas the CG engaged in their usual activities. Anxiety levels were assessed for both groups at baseline and after the intervention. The researcher observed behaviors before, during, and after the intervention, which compared IML with routine activities, using the Behavioral Observation Form.
Participants in the EG exhibited a significantly lower mean anxiety score compared to the CG after 4 weeks of IML. In addition, behaviors such as smiling, joyfulness, appearing relaxed, calmness, music recognition, singing, following the rhythm, and making eye contact were significantly more frequent in the EG than in the CG.
IML can significantly reduce anxiety levels and enhance positive behaviors associated with mood, relaxation, connection to music, and social engagement in people with dementia. Care workers in community settings, such as those involving DCSS, may adopt this study's protocol to provide IML to people with dementia who enjoy music.

title: Patient-Specific Clinical Formulation for Agitation in Alzheimer's Disease: Beyond Group-Level Evidence.
abstract: Agitation in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is clinically heterogeneous. Patients who meet the same syndromic definition can differ in the behaviour of greatest concern, the factors that precipitate or sustain it, the risks involved and their response to treatment. Randomised trials are essential for estimating average treatment effects; individual treatment selection also requires patient-specific clinical information. This review considers patient-specific clinical formulation as a practical way to connect group-level evidence with individual treatment decisions. The formulation makes explicit what is being treated, which contributors are plausible, which contextual or reversible factors matter, what outcome would count as meaningful improvement and when treatment should be changed or stopped. Treatment response then becomes additional clinical information: early benefit, adverse effects or an unexpected course may support or call into question the initial formulation. Non-pharmacological care and treatment of reversible causes remain the foundation of management, with medication reserved for agitation that is severe, persistent, dangerous or highly distressing. For Japan, we propose a formulation summary as a prototype for shared documentation across care settings; its feasibility and clinical value require prospective evaluation. Moving beyond group averages entails applying evidence more carefully to the needs of the individual patient.

title: Empowered by participation: Patients' and caregivers' experiences in the law clinic. Multidisciplinary dementia research at the intersection of law and medicine.
abstract: BackgroundA pilot study, the Law Clinic, implemented extensive cognitive, neuropsychiatric, and legal assessments within an interdisciplinary framework. A study design of this kind has not been previously applied. The study was necessary to generate knowledge on the relationship between symptoms of dementia and patients' legal status.ObjectiveThe pilot aimed to determine, through participants' experiences, whether expanding such multi-component research is ethically sustainable, and whether clinical studies that combine medical and legal perspectives of this nature can feasibly be conducted.Methods20 people with Alzheimer's disease and related disorders and 20 caregivers (spouses) participated in the study, which included several assessments and interviews for both parties. In the final interview, participants reflected on their experiences participating in the study. The transcribed material was analyzed using inductive content analysis to identify key themes related to participation and perceived burden.ResultsParticipants reported positive experiences, with 90% indicating no burden. Most described the study as meaningful, empowering, and even enjoyable. Separate interviews for patients and caregivers were considered essential for open communication and comprehensive perspectives. The findings support scaling up the Law Clinic Study.ConclusionsThe novel Law Clinic Study protocol proved sustainable and feasible. Thoughtful design, and multidisciplinary expertise can ensure respectful and meaningful engagement in research for people with Alzheimer's disease and related disorders and their caregivers. Our findings suggest that research addressing complex and sensitive issues through broad interdisciplinary methods can be ethically sound, generate unique knowledge that would otherwise remain inaccessible, and may even prove empowering for participants.

title: Why do some patients adhere worse? The role of frailty and depression in Parkinson disease.
abstract:
To investigate associations of frailty, depression, disease severity, and sociodemographic factors with treatment adherence, health behaviours, and disease-related knowledge in patients with Parkinson disease (PD), and to examine the relationship between health behaviours and quality of life.
The study included 99 patients with PD (mean age: 70.11 ± 5.5 years; mean disease duration: 8.3 ± 5.68 years), all classified as Hoehn and Yahr stage 2 or higher. Standardized assessment tools included the Parkinson Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39), Schwab and England Activities of Daily Living Scale (SE-ADL), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Adherence to Refills and Medications Scale (ARMS), Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI), Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), Health Behaviour Inventory (HBI), and an author-designed clinical and sociodemographic questionnaire.
Frailty was identified in 86.37% of participants. Non-frail patients demonstrated significantly better health behaviours (89.38 ± 8.25 vs 82.58 ± 10.16, p < 0.05) and treatment adherence (15.62 ± 2.18 vs 18.64 ± 4.08, p < 0.05) than frail patients. Better functional status was associated with higher treatment adherence (p < 0.001, ρ=-0.402), whereas greater severity of depressive symptoms was associated with poorer adherence (p < 0.001, ρ=0.352). Older patients were less likely to use the Internet to obtain information about PD (77.42% for 65 y.o, 41.94% for 66-70 y.o. and 24.32% for >70 y.o. group, p < 0.001), while higher educational attainment was positively associated with expanding knowledge about the disease (from 97.14% for higher education to 50% for primary, p = 0.001).
Frailty, depressive symptoms, disease severity, and sociodemographic factors were associated with treatment adherence and health behaviours in patients with PD. Non-frail patients showed better adherence and healthier behaviours, while greater depressive symptom severity was associated with poorer adherence.
Comprehensive PD care should address psychosocial, emotional, and behavioural factors alongside neurological management to support treatment adherence and patient care.

title: Is it safe-and ethical-to prescribe THC to youth?
abstract: The medical use of cannabis-derived products in children and adolescents has expanded beyond established indications for purified cannabidiol (CBD), with increasing investigation of CBD-rich extracts containing Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) for neuropsychiatric conditions. Although preliminary studies suggest potential symptomatic benefits, the evidence remains limited by small samples, heterogeneous formulations, short follow-up, and insufficient assessment of long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. Unlike CBD, THC directly activates CB1 receptors as a partial agonist, a pharmacological property underlying both its therapeutic and psychoactive effects. Following oral administration, THC undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism to the psychoactive metabolite 11-hydroxy-THC, with substantial interindividual variability in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics supporting individualized dosing according to clinical response and tolerability. Experimental studies raise concerns regarding THC exposure during neurodevelopment, while observational studies associate frequent, high-potency recreational cannabis use with cognitive impairment, psychosis, and other adverse psychiatric outcomes. These findings cannot be directly extrapolated to regulated medicinal cannabinoid use, which differs substantially in product composition, dosing, administration, therapeutic indication, and clinical monitoring. Nevertheless, long-term neurodevelopmental safety data for medicinal THC exposure in children and adolescents remain limited. These uncertainties must be weighed against the consequences of inadequately treated disease, particularly severe drug-resistant epilepsy. Accordingly, the risk-benefit assessment of THC-containing products should be individualized, considering disease severity, treatment refractoriness, available evidence-based alternatives, therapeutic response, and tolerability. Long-term prospective studies and improved patient-selection strategies are needed to better define the role of THC-containing medicinal products in pediatric populations.

title: Mental Health Outcomes Among Transgender People in South Africa During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Service Disruptions and Social, Structural, and Relational Correlates.
abstract:
We examined how sociodemographic, structural, and violence-related factors and disruptions in HIV services and gender-affirming care (GAC: nonmedical supplies, therapy/counseling, medications/hormones, surgeries) were associated with suicidal ideation and moderate/severe anxiety and depression symptoms among South African transgender people.
In September-November 2021, surveyors sampled populations with high HIV risk to understand COVID-19 pandemic experiences. We analyzed sociodemographic, structural (housing, food, financial insecurities), and violence correlates of suicidal ideation and anxiety and depression symptoms. We estimated associations of disruptions in HIV services and GAC with suicidal ideation and anxiety and depression symptoms, adjusting for identified correlates. Additional analyses were stratified by HIV status and age (15-24, 25-30, >30).
Among 194 transgender people, 27% (N = 190) reported suicidal ideation and 37% (N = 178) reported anxiety and depression symptoms. Factors positively associated with suicidal ideation included living with disabilities, increasing educational attainment, unemployment, financial and housing insecurity, and emotional violence; social and structural vulnerabilities affected nearly all HIV and age strata. Correlates positively associated with moderate/severe anxiety and depression symptoms comprised age, housing insecurity, and economic violence. Disruptions in gender-affirming therapy/counseling, medications/hormones, and/or surgeries were positively associated with moderate/severe anxiety and depression symptoms (overall; people without HIV; aged 15-24, 25-30) and suicidal ideation (aged 15-24). In those reporting HIV service disruptions, suicidal ideation (overall, aged 15-24) and anxiety and depression symptoms (overall, aged 25-30) were higher.
Social and structural inequalities were associated with suicidal ideation; GAC and HIV service disruptions were mostly associated with moderate/severe anxiety and depression symptoms. Improving transgender people's mental health requires reducing inequalities while preserving care linkages and access.

title: Comorbidities and infectious episodes in multiple sclerosis patients within general practices in the Netherlands.
abstract:
People with multiple sclerosis (PwMS) are at heightened risk of comorbidities and infections, due to the disease's debilitating nature and side effects of disease-modifying therapies (DMT).
This retrospective case-control study was conducted the Dutch Nivel Primary Care Database from the year 2019, assessing chronic comorbidities and infections in PwMS versus matched controls. The influence of the comorbidity burden (evaluated by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)) and infections on mortality was evaluated using Cox regression.
A higher lifetime prevalence of chronic diseases in PwMS was found, in particular for osteoporosis, stroke, epilepsy, peripheral artery disease, glaucoma, depression and certain oncological diseases (e.g. kidney, hematological, skin cancers). Comorbidity burden was higher in male PwMS, older age, prolonged disease duration, and lower socio-economic status (SES). The crude annual infection rate was higher in PwMS than in matched controls (OR 1.86; 95% CI 1.73 - 1.99). CCI scores of 1 and ≥2 were associated with significantly increased 5-year mortality (aHR 1.86 and 3.30, respectively), as was having at least one infectious episode in 2019 (aHR 1.68).
PwMS have more chronic comorbidities and are at a considerable heightened risk of infections. Prevention, early detection and treatment of comorbidities may ameliorate prognosis of MS and the presence of comorbidities should be part of individualized DMT MS patient care.

title: Antibody-Dependent Cellular Phagocytosis and Cytotoxicity in Patients With LGI1 and CASPR2 Encephalitis.
abstract:
Antibodies against LGI1 and CASPR2 (LGI1/CASPR2-IgG) associate with forms of autoimmune encephalitis (AE) that improve with immunotherapy but often show long-term residual disability. We aimed to investigate whether autoantibody effector functions contribute to pathogenic mechanisms and might act as prognostic biomarkers in patients with LGI1/CASPR2-AE.
We included patients with LGI1/CASPR2-AE, sufficient clinical information, and 1 serum sample available. We assessed the functional profile of LGI1/CASPR2-IgG using in vitro cell-based assays for complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP), and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). Outcome was measured using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and the Clinical Assessment Scale in AE.
We enrolled 55 patients (LGI1 = 31 and CASPR2 = 24). Coexistent ADCC and ADCP (ADCC+/ADCP+) were found in 28/55 patients (10/31 with LGI1 and 18/24 with CASPR2), while an isolated ADCP (ADCC-/ADCP+) was detected in 15 patients (12 with LGI1-IgG and 3 with CASPR2-IgG), and an isolated ADCC (ADCC+/ADCP-) was detected in 2 LGI1-IgG-positive patients. Because most patients (84%) showed a combination of IgG1/IgG3 and IgG4 subclass, no specific functional profiles could be identified according to the predominant subclass. Quantitative ADCP levels showed only a moderate correlation with CASPR2/LGI1-IgG titers (rho = 0.35, p = 0.02), while ADCC showed a moderate/strong correlation (rho = 0.54, p = 0.002). None of the patients showed CDC activation. In a multivariate logistic regression model (including functional profile, rituximab treatment, relapsing course, and cognitive impairment at onset), the ADCC+/ADCP + profile was the only predictor of poor outcome (mRS > 1, OR: 10.97 [95% CI 1.96-106.9]; p = 0.014).
ADCC and ADCP, but not CDC, are common effector functions of LGI1/CASPR2-IgG, and their presence correlates with long-term poor outcome, suggesting that they might represent a useful prognostic biomarker and suggest additional pathogenic mechanisms. We provide the proof- of principle for a framework that could be applied to other autoantibody-mediated disorders.

title: Prevalence and Correlates of Joint Pain in Chicago Midlife Women With HIV: A Cross-sectional Study.
abstract: Joint pain is among the most common and disabling forms of chronic pain in women. Whether joint pain is more prevalent among women with versus without HIV (WWH/WWoH) and contributes to greater impairment is unknown. The Pain, Enjoyment, and General Activity instrument assessed joint pain in midlife WWH versus WWoH to determine associations with frailty, loneliness, and depressive/anxiety symptoms. Moderate/severe pain was more commonly reported in WWH than WWoH (44.1 vs. 38.3%) but not significantly. Women with moderate/severe joint pain were more likely to be prefrail/frail (aOR 3.05; confidence interval [CI]: 1.65-5.63) and report greater depressive symptomology (aOR 2.42; CI: 1.31-4.47), anxiety (aOR 3.38; CI: 1.53-7.43), and loneliness (aOR 1.84; CI: 1.02-3.29). Joint pain is highly prevalent in mid-life WWH and WWoH and associated with frailty, depression, anxiety, and loneliness. Identifying and addressing joint pain and associated conditions may improve multiple health domains in midlife women with and without HIV.

title: The impact of religiosity and spirituality on health outcomes and decision making among African Americans with epilepsy: A review of direct and indirect evidence.
abstract: Epilepsy is a common neurological disorder in the United States that disproportionately affects African Americans. Religious and spiritual practices are important coping mechanisms that may influence health beliefs and healthcare decisions, yet their influence on epilepsy outcomes in this population remains understudied. This narrative review examines how religious and spiritual practices contribute to health decision making behaviors among African Americans living with epilepsy. A literature search was conducted using PubMed, Google Scholar, Connected Papers, and the New York University Library system, focusing on religiosity and spirituality in chronic illness, epilepsy outcomes, racial disparities, stigma in faith-based settings, and church-based health interventions. Across the reviewed literature, findings showed that religiosity and spirituality were associated with coping, finding purpose, social support, and quality of life. In epilepsy-specific studies, positive religious and spiritual coping associated with better well-being, lower anxiety and depressive symptoms, and higher quality of life, while negative religious coping was associated with poorer psychosocial outcomes. Direct evidence among African Americans with epilepsy was limited; however, available findings suggest that Black patients relied more on religion, emotional support, positive reframing, and denial as coping strategies compared to White patients. Overall, this review highlights the need to better understand how African Americans with epilepsy use religious and spiritual frameworks to manage living with a chronic neurological condition.

title: Depression in people with epilepsy: reliability and validity of the Czech version of Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) and Beck Depression Fast Screen (BDI-FS) for major depressive episode.
abstract:
Depression affects up to 55% of people with epilepsy (PWE) yet remains systematically underdiagnosed. This study aimed to evaluate the psychometric properties of the Czech versions of the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) and Beck Depression Inventory-Fast Screen (BDI-FS) for identifying major depressive episode (MDE) in PWE.
A cross-sectional study was conducted with n = 278 adult PWE, assessed at the tertiary epilepsy center. MDE diagnosis was established using the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (M.I.N.I. 6.0.0) as the diagnostic gold standard. Psychometric evaluation included internal consistency, test-retest reliability, exploratory factor analysis, diagnostic accuracy via ROC analysis and concurrent validity against the The Neurological Disorders Depression Inventory for Epilepsy (NDDI-E), The Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ), and QOLIE-89.
25% of the sample (n = 70) met criteria for MDE. Both instruments demonstrated excellent reliability (BDI-II: α = 0.93; BDI-FS: α = 0.81) and strong one-month test-retest stability (ICC = 0.84 and 0.79, respectively). Factor analysis replicated a two-factor structure comprising Somatic-Affective and Cognitive dimensions, accounting for 44% of total variance. Both scales correlated strongly with the NDDI-E (ρ ≈ 0.74) and showed expected negative strong correlations with functional capacity and quality of life. ROC analysis identified optimal cutoffs of BDI-II > 14 (AUC = 0.984, sensitivity 95.7%, specificity 95.1%) and BDI-FS > 3 (AUC = 0.925, sensitivity 84.3%, specificity 85.6%).
The Czech BDI-II version and its brief alternative BDI-FS are reliable and valid instruments for screening MDE in epilepsy. Implementation of these tools in epilepsy clinics may substantially improve depression detection and patient outcomes.

title: Presenting and residual movement disorders in all-cause autoimmune encephalitis.
abstract:
Movement disorders are among the most common autoimmune encephalitis (AE) symptoms, yet their detailed phenomenology and impact remain underexplored.
We evaluated the prevalence, characteristics, and impact of movement disorders at presentation and latest follow-up in all-cause AE.
We retrospectively reviewed AE patients from a tertiary neuroimmunology clinic. Movement disorders were characterized at presentation and latest follow-up and compared between antibody-positive and antibody-negative disease. Outcomes were assessed using the Modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and the Clinical Assessment Scale in Autoimmune Encephalitis (CASE).
Sixty-eight patients were included (53% female, average age 54 years, SD 20.1, 50% antibody-positive). Thirty-seven (52%) patients had movement disorders at presentation, of whom 23 (34%) had residual movement disorders at latest follow-up. The most common movement disorders at presentation included dystonia, ataxia, stereotypies, and catatonia. The most common residual movement disorders included ataxia, dystonia and parkinsonism. Antibody-negative patients were less likely to present with movement disorders (p = 0.02). Patients with movement disorders at presentation were more likely to be women (p = 0.04), had longer time to first outpatient visit (p = 0.04), and had higher mRS score and CASE Score at presentation (mRS 3.32 vs 2.52, p = 0.015, CASE 6.27 vs 4.39, p = 0.094) and at follow-up (mRS 2.19 vs 1.25, p = 0.017, CASE 2.53 vs 1.28, p = 0.029).
More than half the patients with movement disorders had residual symptoms. Antibody-negative patients were less likely to present with movement disorders. Presence of movement disorders at presentation was associated with poorer overall outcomes.

title: Loss of microglial ATM drives synaptic pruning and cognitive impairment in epilepsy.
abstract: Microglia are the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, highly sensitive to oxidative stress and essential for maintaining synaptic homeostasis. While epilepsy induces profound redox imbalance, how oxidative stress reshapes microglial function and disrupts synaptic integrity remains unclear. Here we show that epileptic seizures drive early loss of ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) protein in microglia, independent of canonical DNA damage responses. ATM deficiency shifts microglia into a hyperphagocytic state, with morphological activation and aberrant synaptic engulfment. Single-nucleus transcriptomic analysis of human temporal lobe epilepsy samples reveals that microglial subpopulations with reduced ATM expression display transcriptional signatures of activation, enhanced lysosomal processing, and synapse remodeling, accompanied by extensive rewiring of ligand-receptor interactions with neurons. Restoring ATM in microglia attenuates aberrant phagocytic activity and rescues synaptic integrity and cognitive function. Mechanistically, ATM sustains CREB phosphorylation to maintain G6PD-dependent NADPH production and antioxidant capacity, the disruption of which precipitates mitochondrial oxidative injury and excessive microglial synaptic pruning. Together, our findings reveal a DNA damage-independent ATM-CREB-G6PD axis that limits oxidative stress and maladaptive microglial phagocytosis, highlighting ATM loss as a key driver of synaptic pathology in epilepsy.

title: Serotonergic Toxicity and Hyponatremia Associated with Antidepressant Therapy: The Pivotal Role of SIADH.
abstract: Serotonin syndrome (SS) and the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) are well-recognized adverse drug reactions (ADRs) associated with serotonergic agents, particularly antidepressants. Although traditionally regarded as distinct clinical entities, accumulating evidence suggests that SIADH may represent a key pathophysiological link between serotonergic toxicity and acute hyponatremia, thereby explaining their frequent clinical overlap and, in some cases, severe or fatal outcomes. Excessive serotonergic activity can stimulate hypothalamic pathways regulating arginine vasopressin secretion, resulting in euvolemic hyponatremia and hyponatremic encephalopathy while simultaneously producing the characteristic neuromuscular, autonomic, and mental status abnormalities of SS. This narrative review examines the shared pathophysiological mechanisms, clinical manifestations, diagnostic challenges, and therapeutic implications of SS and SIADH-associated hyponatremia. A comprehensive literature search was conducted, including reviews, pharmacological studies, and case reports involving antidepressants, opioids, antihistamines, nutraceuticals, and emerging serotonergic agents such as ketamine, esketamine, and psilocybin. Particular attention is given to medication combinations, over-the-counter medications, and dietary supplements that may increase serotonergic burden through pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic interactions. The review highlights SIADH as the "thin red line" connecting serotonergic excess with rapid-onset hyponatremia and emphasizes the diagnostic complexity arising from the overlap between neurological manifestations of SS and metabolic encephalopathy secondary to hyponatremia. It also underscores the importance of a systematic diagnostic evaluation of suspected SIADH, including assessment of serum and urinary osmolality and urinary sodium concentration. In published case reports, the absence of urinary osmolality measurements frequently precludes confirmation of SIADH according to established diagnostic criteria, limiting the diagnosis to a possible or probable form rather than a definitive one. Greater awareness of this pathophysiological interplay is essential for early recognition, accurate differential diagnosis, risk stratification, and prevention of severe outcomes through careful medication review, appropriate laboratory evaluation, electrolyte monitoring, and prompt discontinuation of offending agents.

title: Proximity to Water Pollutant Facilities and Risk of Incident Progressive Supranuclear Palsy: Nested Case-Control Study of the UK Biobank.
abstract:
Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a tauopathy of unknown etiology. Environmental toxin exposure is implicated as a risk factor. The aim of our study was to evaluate whether residential proximity to water pollutant-emitting industrial facilities is associated with incident PSP diagnosis.
Within the prospective, population-based UK Biobank cohort, we compared incident PSP cases and age- and sex-matched controls by baseline residential proximity to facilities in the European Pollutant Release and Transfer Register (PRTR).
Among 221 incident PSP cases (mean [SD] age, 63.0 [5.5] years; 91 women [41.2%]) and 2,249 controls, increased PSP risk was associated with proximity to facilities emitting heavy metals (odds ratio [OR] 1.38; 95% CI 1.03-1.85), pesticides (OR 1.66; 95% CI 1.12-2.46), other organic pollutants (OR 1.52; 95% CI 1.13-2.04), and other inorganic pollutants (OR 1.60; 95% CI 1.19-2.15), after false discovery rate correction. Risk decreased linearly with greater distance (5-10 km), and that residence exceeding 40 years conferred increased risk for heavy metals and organic and inorganic pollutants, unlike shorter residence windows.
Residential proximity to water pollutant-emitting facilities was associated with incident PSP, with possible evidence of distance-dependent and duration-dependent relationships, supporting a potential role for environmental water pollutants in PSP pathogenesis.
This study provides Class III evidence that baseline residential proximity to water pollutant-emitting facilities reported in the 2007 PRTR is associated with a higher risk of subsequent diagnosis of PSP in the UK Biobank.

title: Accuracy and clinical outcomes of robot-assisted deep brain stimulation lead placement using a floor-mounted robotic navigation system: a prospective multicenter study.
abstract:
The aim of this study was to evaluate clinical data to assess the accuracy and safety of a new robot system used for deep brain stimulation (DBS) lead placement.
A prospective, multicenter, single-arm study included 60 patients indicated for DBS. Patients aged 18-85 years with Parkinson's disease, essential tremor, or dystonia were enrolled. The primary outcome was electrode accuracy at the tip, 40 mm from the tip, and the entry point compared with the planned trajectory. Secondary outcomes included operative time (OT), length of stay (LOS), and perioperative complications through discharge.
The cohort (mean age 67.1 ± 9.9 years) primarily consisted of patients with Parkinson's disease (n = 46). The mean OT was 159.0 ± 26.7 minutes, and the mean LOS was 1.6 ± 1.5 days. The complication rate and return to the operating room rate were both 0%. The mean tip error was 0.8 ± 0.5 mm, error at 40 mm from the tip was 0.4 ± 0.5 mm, and entry point error was 1.0 ± 0.8 mm.
DBS electrode implantation using the new robot-assisted system demonstrated high plan-to-place accuracy comparable or superior to historical frame-based and robotic platforms. The safety profile and operative efficiency, reflected by very low complication rates and similar OT and LOS to published literature, support the system as a viable alternative to standard frame-based stereotaxy.
